claims.text: The baseline system is a zirconium-alloy fuel cladding with an elemental Cr coating deposited directly on the substrate.
Directly deposited elemental Cr coatings are prone to premature failure because of elevated-temperature Cr–Zr interdiffusion.
A CrN interlayer should be deposited between the zirconium-alloy substrate and the elemental Cr coating.
A CrN barrier thickness on the order of 100–300 nm is suitable for the proposed intervention.
The interfacial CrN layer is dense and covalently bonded.
Dense CrN has lower atomic diffusivity for both Cr and Zr than the unmodified coating–substrate interface.
The CrN interlayer will significantly reduce elevated-temperature Cr–Zr interdiffusion.
Suppressing Cr–Zr interdiffusion will preserve the integrity of the elemental Cr coating.
The CrN-interlayered coating will maintain oxidation resistance during subcritical-water exposure below approximately 350°C.
The CrN-interlayered coating will maintain oxidation resistance in steam at temperatures up to approximately 1000°C for 30–60 minutes.
Relative to the direct-Cr baseline, the CrN interlayer will improve coating adhesion after environmental exposure.
Relative to the direct-Cr baseline, the CrN interlayer will sustain oxidation resistance during extended subcritical-water exposure.
Relative to the direct-Cr baseline, the CrN interlayer will sustain oxidation resistance during accident-relevant high-temperature steam exposure.
High-temperature processing can produce substantial diffusion of Zr from a substrate into a metallic coating.
EPMA depth profiling can be used to characterize an interdiffusion zone.
SIMS can quantify Cr and Zr interdiffusion in the proposed coating system.
Performance outside the stated temperature and exposure-time bounds is uncertain.
Optimal CrN thickness, CrN formation parameters, and long-term cyclic thermal stability remain to be experimentally established.
